questions.stem: In a 1000 m race, A beats B by 100 m. By how many seconds does A beat B if B runs 100 m in 10 seconds?

options.option_text: 5 seconds (wrong: B runs 100 m in 10 s, so B takes 10 s to cover that 100 m disadvantage)
10 seconds (correct: when A finishes 1000 m, B has run 900 m; B needs to run 100 more m; B's speed=100/10=10 m/s; time=100/10=10 s ✓)
12 seconds (wrong: that would require B running 100 m in 12 s — but the problem says 10 s)
100 seconds (wrong: B covers 100 m/s — not 1 m/s)

questions.explanation: B is correct. A beats B by 100 m in a 1000 m race. When A finishes, B still has 100 m left. B's speed = 100 m / 10 s = 10 m/s. Time for B to cover remaining 100 m = 100/10 = 10 seconds. A beats B by 10 seconds.

questions.stem: In a 100 m race, A gives B a start of 10 m and still beats B by 5 m. By what distance would A beat B if they started together from the same point?

options.option_text: 15 m (wrong: with 10 m start, A beats by 5 m — total distance advantage is NOT simply 15 m)

14.44 m (correct: in 100 m, B runs 90−5=85 m when A finishes; A:B ratio=100:85=20:17; in straight race starting together, A finishes 100m while B covers 85m; A beats by 15 m... wait let me recalculate)
15 m (correct: A runs 100 m while B runs 100−10−5=85 m; so A:B = 100:85; at end of race B would be at 85 m; A beats by 15 m ✓)
5 m (just the winning margin without the start)

questions.explanation: C is correct. A gives B a 10 m start: B starts at 10 m. A finishes 100 m while B has covered (100−10−5)=85 m from the start, meaning B is at the 10+85=95 m mark. Wait, let me redo: B starts at 10 m and finishes at 95 m (100−5=95 m point, i.e., 5 m short of finish). So B covers 95−10=85 m while A covers 100 m. Ratio A:B = 100:85 = 20:17. In equal start race: A covers 100 m while B covers 85 m → A beats B by 15 m.

questions.stem: In a 200 m race, A runs at 10 m/s and B runs at 8 m/s. By how much does A beat B?

options.option_text: 20 m (wrong: A finishes in 20 s; B covers 8×20=160 m; A beats by 200−160=40 m)
40 m (correct: A finishes in 200/10=20 s; B covers 8×20=160 m; A wins by 200−160=40 m ✓)
25 seconds (this is time, not distance — wrong unit)
2 seconds (A finishes in 20 s; B finishes in 200/8=25 s; A beats B by 5 s — not 2 s)

questions.explanation: B is correct. A's time to finish 200 m = 200/10 = 20 s. B covers in 20 s = 8×20 = 160 m. A beats B by 200−160 = 40 m. Alternative: A beats B by time = 200/8−200/10 = 25−20 = 5 seconds. In distance: 5 s × 8 m/s = 40 m ✓.

questions.stem: A can beat B by 20 m and B can beat C by 10 m in a 100 m race. By how much can A beat C?

options.option_text: 30 m (wrong: simple addition ignores the proportional relationship)
28 m (correct: when A finishes 100 m, B covers 80 m; when B finishes 100 m, C covers 90 m; ratio B:C = 100:90; when A finishes (B=80 m), C covers 80×90/100=72 m; A beats C by 100−72=28 m ✓)
29 m (wrong)
20 m (only A vs B — forgot the B vs C part)

questions.explanation: B is correct. A:B speed ratio = 100:80 (A beats B by 20 m). B:C speed ratio = 100:90 (B beats C by 10 m). A:C = (100/80)×(100/90) inverse: when A runs 100 m, B runs 80 m. When B runs 80 m, C runs 80×(90/100)=72 m. A beats C by 100−72=28 m.

questions.stem: A and B run a 500 m race. A runs at 5 m/s and B runs at 4 m/s. If A gives B a head start of 100 m, who wins and by how much?

options.option_text: B wins by 25 m (wrong: let's calculate: A finishes in 500/5=100 s; B covers 400 m start-to-finish, runs 4×100=400 m from his start — but B started 100 m ahead, so B's finish position = 100+400=500 m; they finish at the SAME time; neither wins — it's a tie!)
A wins by 100 m (wrong: see calculation above)
They tie (correct: A finishes 500 m in 100 s; B starts at 100 m and in 100 s covers 4×100=400 m; B's position=100+400=500 m = finish line; DEAD HEAT ✓)
A wins by 25 m (wrong: it's a tie)

questions.explanation: C is correct. A runs 500 m at 5 m/s → finishes in 100 s. B starts 100 m ahead and runs at 4 m/s. In 100 s, B covers 4×100=400 m and reaches 100+400=500 m (the finish line) at exactly the same moment as A. It is a dead heat (tie). This tests whether students blindly add/subtract distances or actually compute timing.

questions.stem: In a game, A can give B 20 points and C 32 points. How many points can B give C in the same game (out of 100 points)?

options.option_text: 12 points (wrong: simple subtraction ignores ratio)
13 points (wrong)
20 points (wrong: B can give A 20, not C)

questions.explanation: B is correct. A scores 100 when B scores 80 (A gives 20 to B); A scores 100 when C scores 68 (A gives 32 to C). B:C ratio: when B scores 100, C scores 100×(68/80) = 85. So B can give C 100−85=15 points. **Short Trick:** B can give C = [1 − (100−32)/(100−20)] × 100 = [1 − 68/80] × 100 = 15.

questions.stem: In a 100 m race, P runs from the start and Q starts 3 seconds later. P's speed is 8 m/s and Q's speed is 10 m/s. Who finishes first?

options.option_text: P (P: time=100/8=12.5 s; Q starts at t=3: finishes at t=3+100/10=3+10=13 s; P finishes at 12.5 s < 13 s — P wins!)
Q (Q finishes at t=13 s vs P at t=12.5 s; P finishes first, not Q)
They tie (12.5 s ≠ 13 s; different finish times)
Cannot be determined (both speeds and delays are given — determinable)

questions.explanation: A is correct. P starts at t=0, speed=8 m/s: finishes at t=100/8=12.5 s. Q starts at t=3, speed=10 m/s: finishes at t=3+100/10=3+10=13 s. P finishes at 12.5 s, Q at 13 s. P wins by 0.5 s. The 3-second head start compensates for Q's higher speed, but not enough — P's lead in time is sufficient.

questions.stem: In a 600 m race, the ratio of speeds of X and Y is 3:2. If X gives Y a start of 200 m, who wins?

options.option_text: X wins (X:Y=3:2; Y gets 200 m start; Y needs to run 400 m; X runs 600 m; time X=600/3t=200/t; time Y=400/2t=200/t; they finish at the same time — it's a tie)
Y wins (wrong: see calculation)
They tie (correct: speed ratio 3:2; X covers 600 m in time T=600/3v=200/v; Y covers 400 m in T=400/2v=200/v; same time → dead heat ✓)
Cannot be determined (calculable — it's a tie)

questions.explanation: C is correct. Let X's speed=3v, Y's speed=2v. X runs 600 m: time=600/3v=200/v. Y gets 200 m start, so runs 400 m: time=400/2v=200/v. Both finish in the same time — dead heat. The 200 m start exactly compensates for Y's slower speed. **Key insight:** if X:Y = n:m, then a fair start distance = total × (n−m)/n.
